The cross challenges ownership of another believer

Verse 12 quotes four slogans: of Paul, of Apollos, of Cephas, of Christ. Verse 13 answers with three questions, and each expects “no.” Christ is not divided. Paul was not crucified for them. They were not baptized into Paul’s name. No party leader died for them or gave them a name. Verses 14–15 add that Paul baptized few, so no one can claim his name.
Paul's remembered weakness refuses to make eloquence the source of faith

Chapter 1 said the Corinthians were dividing over teachers. Paul answers with how he first spoke to them (verses 1–4). He had no fine speech, and he came in weakness and fear. Verse 5 gives the purpose behind that. Faith that rests on a speaker’s skill rests on human wisdom. He wanted theirs to rest on God’s power. Verse 4 names where that power showed: in the Spirit, not in persuasive words.
Different workers serve growth they cannot produce themselves

Verse 4 repeats the slogans: “I follow Paul” and “I follow Apollos.” Verse 5 asks what these men are, and answers “servants.” Verse 6 gives each his task in three short sentences. Paul planted, Apollos watered, and God gave the increase. Only the third makes anything grow. Verse 7 draws the result: planter and waterer are nothing beside God. Verse 8 adds that the planter and the waterer are one.
Received gifts cannot support boasting as though nothing was given

Verse 6 names the problem: being puffed up for one against another. Verse 7 answers with three questions. Who makes you different? What do you have that you did not receive? If you received it, why boast as if you had not? Each question removes a ground for pride. Verses 8–13 then set their boast beside the apostles’ hunger and insults.
The boundary concerns claimed membership rather than leaving the whole world

An earlier letter said not to keep company with the sexually immoral (verse 9). It could be read as meaning everyone. Verse 10 says that would require leaving the world. Verse 11 limits it to one “who is called a brother.” Verse 12 gives the reason in two questions. Paul has no task of judging outsiders; the assembly judges those within. Verse 13 leaves outsiders to God and tells them to remove the man.
Claimed freedom fails when it becomes another form of control

The saying “All things are lawful for me” stands twice in verse 12. Paul does not deny it; he adds two limits. Not all things are helpful. He also will not be brought under the power of anything. The second limit turns the saying around. A freedom that masters its user is no longer freedom. Verses 19–20 give the ground: the body is not one’s own.
Paul distinguishes commands from advice shaped by present distress

Paul marks his sources through the chapter. Verse 10 is the Lord’s command. Verse 12 is Paul’s own word, “not the Lord.” Verse 25 says he has no command about virgins and gives a judgment. Verse 35 says how to take that judgment. It is for their benefit, and it is not a snare to hold them. Its aim is attention to the Lord without distraction, as verses 32–34 explain.
Knowledge must consider the person whom freedom can wound

Verses 4–6 grant the point of those with knowledge: an idol is nothing. Verse 8 grants that food changes nothing before God. Verse 9 then begins with “but.” The right is real, yet it can trip the weak. Verse 10 gives the case: a weak person sees and copies against conscience. Verse 11 counts the cost: a brother for whom Christ died is destroyed. Verse 12 calls this a sin against Christ.
A right can remain valid even when its holder refuses to use it

Chapter 8 asked the knowing to give up a right for the weak. Chapter 9 shows Paul doing the same with his own right. Verses 4–11 prove that he may be supported. Verse 12 says others use this right over the Corinthians. Then it says he did not use it. His reason is in the same verse: no hindrance to the good news. Verse 14 keeps the right in force, as something the Lord ordained.
Food choices depend on setting and another person's good

Verse 23 repeats “All things are lawful” and adds that not all build up. Verse 24 gives the rule for the cases that follow. Seek the neighbor’s good, not your own. Verses 25–27 apply it one way: eat market meat and a host’s food freely. Verses 28–29 apply it the other way. If someone points out idol food, refrain for that person’s conscience. The food is the same; the neighbor’s good decides.
Remembering the shared meal exposes the shame caused by private advantage

Verse 21 describes the fault: each takes his own supper before others. One goes hungry, and another is drunk. Verse 22 says this shames those who have nothing. Paul then recalls the Lord’s words over bread and cup (verses 23–25). Verse 33 gives the practical order that follows from them. They are to wait for one another. Verse 34 adds that anyone hungry should eat at home first.
The body needs members who appear weaker

Two wrong voices speak in the body. In verses 15–16 a member says it is not part of the body. In verse 21 a member says it does not need another. Verse 22 answers the second voice. The parts that seem weaker are necessary. Verses 23–24 add that we give more honor to the less honorable parts. Verse 25 gives God’s purpose: no division, and the same care for each.
Love tests the value of gifts before their display

Chapter 12 listed gifts such as prophecy, knowledge, and faith (12:8–10). Chapter 13 tests those gifts. Verse 2 takes three of them at their fullest. It imagines all mysteries, all knowledge, and faith to move mountains. The verdict is about the person: “I am nothing.” Verses 4–5 then describe love without envy, boasting, or pride. Those faults appeared in 3:3 and 4:6–7.
Understandable and ordered speech must build the gathered group

Verse 26 describes the meeting: each brings a psalm, a teaching, or a language. The problem is not a lack of gifts. The verse gives one test for all of them: building each other up. Verses 27–28 apply it to languages: two or three, in turn, with an interpreter. Verses 29–31 apply it to prophecy: one by one, so all may learn. Verse 19 showed Paul’s own choice of five understood words. Verse 33 gives the ground: God is not a God of confusion.
Resurrection gives present labor a future beyond death

Verses 12–19 follow one claim to its end. If the dead are not raised, Christ is not raised. Then faith is useless, and the dead in Christ have perished (verses 17–18). Verse 20 breaks in with “But now.” Christ has been raised, and he is called the first fruit. A first fruit is the first part of a harvest, with more to come. Verse 23 gives the order: Christ first, then those who are his.
Love governs material help, visiting workers, and shared recognition

Verse 13 gives four short commands. Watch, stand firm, be courageous, be strong. Verse 14 adds a fifth: all is to be done in love. The letter dealt with parties (1:12) and lawsuits (6:6). Chapter 13 described what love does. Verse 14 applies it to “all that you do.”
